paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today, the ruins of Titris Hoyuk, a city built in about 1500 BC, lie silent and buried in southeastern Turkey. But the ruins speak to archaeologists of a time when a revolutionary idea began to shape the cities of the world. Mapping the site of Titris, a team of University of California archaeologists are finding an assortment of urban remains. At the centre of the city, on high ground, once stood a palace and other public buildings, as was usual at the time. From that point, streets radiated out through residential neighbourhoods. Beyond the city walls lay a cemetery and suburbs. On closer examination, the team have found surprises. The whole city seems to follow a master plan. We can therefore conclude that Titris, with a population of 10,000 at its height, represents a striking example of urban planning in ancient times. There was a centralised vision of what a city should look like that appears remarkably similar to typical master-planned communities in the modern world.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Scholars long ago established that the first cities arose about 5,000 years ago in an area known as Mesopotamia that is part of present-day Iraq. Urban development was presumably an outgrowth of increasingly productive farming. Crop surpluses were evidently the key, as they led to the expansion of long-distance trade and allowed people to specialise in crafts such as textile- and ceramic-making. As the number of merchants and artisans grew, farm villages developed over time into cities. By the middle of the third millennium BC, the experiments in city living were such resounding successes that people were flocking to new cities over the entire region of what is now Syria, northern Iraq and Turkey. The Titris excavation, and clues from other similar sites in northern Mesopotamia, suggest that this popular demand led to organised and well-designed construction projects. Only in this way could growing populations' needs be satisfied fast enough.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The Titris excavations are especially revealing of the form, structure and organisation of these earliest cities. The team is concentrating its research on the neighbourhoods and households where most people lived, not on the palaces and temples archaeologists usually focus on. Titris rose and fell over a 300-year period, and then, for reasons which have been obscured by the passage of time, it was totally abandoned and never again reoccupied. Thus, history appears to have simplified the task for archaeologists, because of Titris's failure as a city. In contrast to most other ancient population centres, its ruins are not obscured by layers of debris and later sites one on top of the other. The remnants of Titris lie less than three feet beneath the surface of the earth today.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Even so, archaeologists working at Titris have excavated only small sections of two neighbourhoods, a tiny portion of the old city. To date, they have mapped the buried foundations of about half of the 125-acre site, using hand-held magnetometers (devices which measure magnetic force). Outlines of the city's footprint can be readily plotted because the non-magnetic limestone foundations of buildings stand out clearly from the surrounding iron-rich, magnetic soils. Careful analysis of the resulting magnetometry maps and other findings from the actual excavations of representative areas suggest that Titris was a planned community that was built in one go.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Excavations at the eastern end of Titris exposed large, multi-roomed houses aligned along central streets. The way in which the streets had been planned and the arrangement of these houses, with their regularity and constructional details, clearly demonstrated the existence of some sort of template. The streets had been carefully prepared, first cut into the soil and then paved with rocks, stones and small pot fragments. It was clear that they had been created prior to the construction of the houses at either side.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One well-documented house consisted of 15 rooms, opening out around a courtyard, which was subdivided with low partition walls defining what appeared to be four separate areas. People apparently entered the house through a doorway directly off the street. This house plan, the archaeologists say, appears to be characteristic of Titris domestic buildings, although some houses were smaller variations on the same design. All the houses were probably occupied by extended families, for each contained several cooking areas, and all the evidence indicates that many were used for more than just residential purposes. Some of the ruined houses contain oval basins which archaeologists think were used for washing and treating sheep's wool. Among the artefacts in several houses were stone weights, no doubt associated with weaving textiles. One aspect of Titris houses was unlike anything usually associated with typical modern residences; each household had a tomb where the family dead were placed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The spread of urbanisation and city planning in ancient Mesopotamia probably reflected a high degree of social organisation and complexity and the presence of powerful rulers, who wanted to expand and strengthen their bases of power and had the financial means to do it. The rise of planned cities seems to have coincided with such transforming innovations as writing, the use of animals for traction, wheeled carts, metallurgy and craft specialisation. The most elemental, if less materialistic, reason for people being inclined to congregate in planned cities in ancient Mesopotamia and ever since seems to be that humans simply like to live and work in groups. Cities have always been centres of learning and excitement, places for doing things and making one's mark.
